Real data: chr19 association testing with binary, continuous, and count phenotypes

Source: vignettes/real-data-chr19.Rmd
real-data-chr19.Rmd

Overview

This vignette runs the complete Step 1 → 2 → 3 pipeline on real genotype data from the Jackson Heart Study (JHS) cohort — chromosome 19, 3 313 samples, local ancestry inferred as African (AFR) / European (EUR) — and demonstrates ancestry_smmat() with all three response types GMMAT supports: binary (logistic), continuous (linear), and count (Poisson). Only the family argument (and the simulated phenotype) changes between them; everything else about the call is identical, which is the point — swap those two inputs and the same code handles your own binary, continuous, or count phenotype.

  • For matrix-level intuition on the two splitting methods, see vignette("split-intuition").
  • For building ancestry_split() inputs from your own VCF + MSP files (including K > 2 populations), see vignette("toy-vcf-msp-example") — this JHS cohort only has AFR/EUR calls, so Steps 1–2 below are shown for two populations, but nothing changes for K > 2 beyond the MSP header.
# Step 1: split. Step 2: write one GDS per population.
split_real <- ancestry_split(
  vcf_path = file.path(RAW, "LANTERN.phased.bcf"),
  msp_path = file.path(RAW, "LANTERN_chr19.msp.tsv.gz"),
  mode     = "dosage",
  chrom    = "chr19",
  verbose  = TRUE
)
#> === LANTERN Ancestry Split (Step 1, mode = dosage) ===
#> Step 1: Parsing RFMix MSP file...
#>   Parsing MSP file: ../../raw/LANTERN_chr19.msp.tsv.gz
#>     Found 3416 samples, 2 populations
#>     Pop codes: AFR = 0, EUR = 1
#>   MSP samples: 3416  Tracts: 653
#> 
#> Step 2: Querying VCF sample IDs...
#>   VCF samples: 3314
#> 
#> Step 3: Intersecting samples...
#>   Common: 3313
#> 
#> Step 4: Parsing VCF genotypes...
#>   44275 variant lines read
#> 
#> Step 5: Mapping variants to ancestry tracts...
#>   Filtered to chrom chr19: 44275 variants
#>   Variants with no tract: 2 (dropped)
#> 
#> Step 6: Broadcasting ancestry to variants...
#> 
#> Step 7: Splitting genotypes by ancestry (dosage)...
#> 
#> Step 8: Filtering monomorphic variants...
#>   Removed 2 monomorphic variants
#> 
#> === Step 1 Complete: 44271 variants, 3313 samples, 2 populations ===
gds_paths <- write_ancestry_gds(split_real, tempfile(), verbose = TRUE)
#> === LANTERN Write Ancestry GDS (Step 2) ===
#> Writing GDS for AFR (1/2)...
#> Writing GDS for EUR (2/2)...
#> 
#> === Step 2 Complete: 2 GDS file(s) written to /tmp/Rtmp7oMjf3/file699222c4d9016 ===

ids <- split_real$sample_ids
cat("Samples:", length(ids), "\n")
#> Samples: 3313

1 Gene-group file and kinship

The full chr19 gene-group file covers 1 442 genes; to keep this vignette fast we use a 5-gene subset here (the pattern is identical for the full file — just point gene_group_file at it and expect several minutes per SMMAT() call instead of seconds).

genes_full  <- read.table(file.path(RAW, "genes_chr19_smmat.tsv"), header = FALSE,
                           sep = "\t",
                           col.names = c("gene", "chrom", "pos", "ref", "alt", "weight"))
genes_small <- genes_full[genes_full$gene %in% unique(genes_full$gene)[1:5], ]

kinship <- readRDS(file.path(RAW, "LANTERN_kinship_rds.rds"))
common_ids <- intersect(ids, rownames(kinship))
cat("Genes:", length(unique(genes_small$gene)), "  Common samples:", length(common_ids), "\n")
#> Genes: 5   Common samples: 3313

genes_small is passed straight to ancestry_smmat()’s gene_group_file argument below as a data.frame — no tempfile()/write.table()/unlink() needed; ancestry_smmat() manages the temporary file GMMAT requires internally and cleans it up automatically. A plain file path still works too, if that’s more convenient for your own pipeline.

2 Binary phenotype (family = binomial()) 

set.seed(1)
pheno_binary <- data.frame(id = common_ids, y = rbinom(length(common_ids), 1, 0.3))

res_binary <- ancestry_smmat(gds_paths, pheno_binary, y ~ 1, kinship, genes_small,
                              family    = binomial(link = "logit"),
                              MAF.range = c(0, 0.05), verbose = FALSE)
print(res_binary$results)
#>      gene     p_AFR     p_EUR  p_cauchy
#> 1    A1BG 0.1492616 0.7938859 0.3997315
#> 2   ABCA7 0.2031324 0.1900808 0.1964182
#> 3 ABHD17A 0.8941616 0.2588411 0.7459638
#> 4   ABHD8 0.5078140 0.3048892 0.3958519
#> 5   ACER1 0.2196545 0.3375616 0.2692847

3 Continuous phenotype (family = gaussian())

Only the family and the simulated y change:

pheno_cont <- data.frame(id = common_ids, y = rnorm(length(common_ids)))

res_cont <- ancestry_smmat(gds_paths, pheno_cont, y ~ 1, kinship, genes_small,
                            family    = gaussian(link = "identity"),
                            MAF.range = c(0, 0.05), verbose = FALSE)
print(res_cont$results)
#>      gene      p_AFR     p_EUR  p_cauchy
#> 1    A1BG 0.32271246 0.5564923 0.4305589
#> 2   ABCA7 0.71670271 0.3862533 0.5684131
#> 3 ABHD17A 0.31455720 0.6888582 0.5024665
#> 4   ABHD8 0.56071838 0.8476944 0.7593479
#> 5   ACER1 0.09634068 0.7767378 0.2485254

4 Count phenotype (family = poisson()) 

pheno_count <- data.frame(id = common_ids, y = rpois(length(common_ids), lambda = 3))

res_count <- ancestry_smmat(gds_paths, pheno_count, y ~ 1, kinship, genes_small,
                             family    = poisson(link = "log"),
                             MAF.range = c(0, 0.05), verbose = FALSE)
print(res_count$results)
#>      gene      p_AFR      p_EUR  p_cauchy
#> 1    A1BG 0.89654667 0.02082793 0.0513362
#> 2   ABCA7 0.45190129 0.66226067 0.5638687
#> 3 ABHD17A 0.29662855 0.75212153 0.5428024
#> 4   ABHD8 0.11031509 0.65554127 0.2321887
#> 5   ACER1 0.04307048 0.81238745 0.1048616

5 Adjusting for covariates

Covariates (age, sex, genotype PCs, batch, …) are just additional terms in formula, as long as the matching columns exist in pheno — nothing else about the call changes. Here we add a simulated age and sex to the continuous-phenotype example from Section 3:

set.seed(2)
age <- round(rnorm(length(common_ids), mean = 55, sd = 12))
sex <- factor(sample(c("F", "M"), length(common_ids), replace = TRUE))
pheno_cov <- data.frame(id = common_ids, y = rnorm(length(common_ids)),
                         age = age, sex = sex)

res_cov <- ancestry_smmat(gds_paths, pheno_cov, y ~ age + sex, kinship, genes_small,
                           family    = gaussian(link = "identity"),
                           MAF.range = c(0, 0.05), verbose = FALSE)
print(res_cov$results)
#>      gene      p_AFR      p_EUR   p_cauchy
#> 1    A1BG 0.78973635 0.63646754 0.72827528
#> 2   ABCA7 0.61704448 0.70291389 0.66320132
#> 3 ABHD17A 0.05755877 0.08958273 0.07014252
#> 4   ABHD8 0.61776792 0.42714304 0.52459912
#> 5   ACER1 0.10424888 0.90977046 0.57638538

Genotype PCs from your own PCA (e.g. PC1, …, PC10) work the same way: add them as columns to pheno and to formula (y ~ age + sex + PC1 + PC2 + ...).

6 Where to get gene-group files for other species/builds

ancestry_smmat()’s gene_group_file (a data.frame or a path — both resolve to the same six columns, no header: gene chrom pos ref alt weight) is fundamentally your own called variants intersected with gene boundaries — it’s specific to your VCF, not something you download ready-made for an arbitrary variant set. genes_full, used above, was built exactly this way: gene coordinates for chr19 intersected against the JHS variant positions.

What you can download are the gene/exon coordinate annotations to intersect against your own variants (e.g. with bedtools intersect or a GTF-parsing script), for human or any other species:

  • Ensembl BioMart — gene/exon coordinates for hundreds of species (GRCh37/GRCh38 human builds included); the classic way to export a custom gene coordinate table.
  • GENCODE — comprehensive human and mouse gene annotation (GTF/GFF3), the reference set most rare-variant pipelines build their gene definitions from.
  • UCSC Table Browser — RefSeq/ Ensembl/GENCODE gene tables for many species and genome builds, with a web UI for filtering/exporting BED files directly.
  • NCBI RefSeq — the underlying gene/transcript annotation source Ensembl/UCSC also redistribute.
  • ANNOVAR — if you already annotate variants with ANNOVAR (refGene/ensGene databases), its per-variant gene assignments can be reshaped directly into the gene_group_file format.

Once you have gene boundaries in hand, build the file per chromosome: for each variant in your VCF, look up which gene’s boundary it falls in (chromosome + position), write one row per (gene, variant) pair, and set weight (commonly 1 for an unweighted burden test, or a MAF-based weight — see MAF.weights.beta in ?ancestry_smmat).

7 Other ways to adapt this to your own data

  • More than two populations: nothing above changes structurally — gds_paths just needs one named entry per population (see vignette("toy-vcf-msp-example"), Part B, for building the underlying ancestry_split()/write_ancestry_gds() inputs at K > 2).
  • Full gene set / real analysis: pass genes_full instead of the 5-gene subset as gene_group_file, and pass ancestry_counts = split_real$ancestry_counts / variant_info = split_real$variant_info (from Step 1) to ancestry_smmat() to weight the Cauchy combination by each gene’s local ancestry proportions instead of equal weights.
  • Every GMMAT::SMMAT() argument is available: MAF.range, miss.cutoff, method, and ncores are named parameters here with the same meaning as in a direct SMMAT() call; anything else SMMAT() accepts — tests, rho, MAF.weights.beta, missing.method, use.minor.allele, auto.flip, Garbage.Collection, group.file.sep, meta.file.prefix — forwards through ... unchanged. See ?ancestry_smmat and ?GMMAT::SMMAT.
  • Raw per-population results: every call above also returns $smmat_results, a named list of the untouched GMMAT::SMMAT() data.frames (e.g. res_binary$smmat_results$AFR) if you need columns beyond the summarized p_<POP>/p_cauchy in $results — burden-only p-values, variant counts, allele frequencies, etc.
